passage:
"So you really left the bank to make furniture?" Parveen asked, running her hand along a half-sanded table in Santosh's workshop.
"Not at first," Santosh said, blowing sawdust off a chisel. "First I did weekend classes for a year. Kept my job. Made three terrible stools."
"That's what I'm scared of. Quitting and then finding out I hate it."
"Then don't quit. What have you tried so far?"
"Nothing. Just... dreamt about it. Watched videos."
"Videos don't give you splinters," Santosh laughed. "There's a Saturday beginners' batch here. Six weeks. You'll know a lot by the end."
"And my job?"
"Keep it. Six Saturdays costs you some sleep, not your career."
Parveen picked up a small offcut and turned it over. "Can I sign up today?"
"Sign up, and come back and tell me if you still love it after the third Saturday. That's usually when people find out."

qa.q: How long is the Saturday beginners' batch?
qa.a: It is six weeks.

qa.q: What was Parveen afraid of before visiting the workshop?
qa.a: Parveen was afraid of quitting her job and then discovering she hated woodworking.

qa.q: Why is the Saturday batch a wise next step for Parveen?
qa.a: It is a small, low-cost test that gives real feedback about woodworking while she keeps her job, so no bridges are burned.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Parveen's question about signing up today?
qa.a: Santosh probably feels pleased and a little amused, recognising the same eagerness Santosh had before that first year of weekend classes.

grounding: Shows a young adult testing a new direction cheaply by talking with someone doing what she admires and joining a short weekend course while keeping her job.

passage: Keerthana smiled at the recorder her friend Kalyani had set up for the college alumni podcast. "Okay, I'm Keerthana, batch of 2021, and a year ago I'd have said I was the most behind person in our class. No startup, no husband, no foreign degree. I used to check everyone's updates every night and feel sick. What changed? Honestly, my grandmother. She started teaching at fifty-two, after raising four kids, and taught for twenty years. When I told her I felt late, she laughed. So now I plan in years. This year, I'm learning data work properly. In three years, I'd like to lead a small team at a place that treats people well. I don't measure myself against the reunion slideshow anymore. I ask: was I honest, did I learn, was I kind? Some weeks the answer's no. But I'm not in a race, Kalyani. I'm on my own road."

qa.q: At what age did Keerthana's grandmother start teaching?
qa.a: She started teaching at fifty-two.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel about her progress now compared with a year ago?
qa.a: Keerthana feels calmer and more content, no longer sick with comparison, because she measures herself by her own values.

qa.q: What habit helps Keerthana stay on her own timeline?
qa.a: She plans in years, not weeks, and checks herself against her own questions about honesty, learning and kindness instead of others' updates.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel recording this for the podcast?
qa.a: Kalyani may feel inspired and glad, perhaps reflecting on a personal timeline, and hopeful that listeners who feel behind will find comfort in it.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding comfort in uneven life paths, planning in years and measuring progress against her own values.

passage:
[Voice note, sent 11:40 pm]
"Deepak! It's Kalyani, obviously. Day four in Pune and I have to tell you everything. The hostel room is tiny but it has a window with a tree, and a crow that visits every morning. I've already been to three cafés, a bookshop that stays open till ten, and a street where they sell vada pav for fifteen rupees. Today we had orientation and I joined the drama club and the photography club, and I think the trekking club, I'm not sure, I signed so many sheets. Everyone is from somewhere different. There's a girl from Shillong on my floor who's already my best friend, probably. Mummy called twice and asked if I'm eating properly and I said yes, yes, bye, I was running to a quiz. I haven't cried once, can you believe it? Okay, I'm going to sleep. Actually, no, they're making instant noodles downstairs, gotta go!"

qa.q: How many cafés has Kalyani been to?
qa.a: Kalyani has already been to three cafés.

qa.q: How does Kalyani seem to feel in her first days in Pune?
qa.a: Kalyani feels thrilled and full of energy, so caught up in new things that there is no time to feel homesick.

qa.q: What small step could help Kalyani later, when the excitement fades?
qa.a: Kalyani could make time for proper calls with Mummy and keep one or two routines from home, so there is a base when the novelty wears off.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel after being told yes, yes, bye?
qa.a: Mummy may feel glad Kalyani is happy but also a little left out and worried whether Kalyani is really eating and resting.

grounding: Shows a student arriving in a new city, excited by everything fresh, with homesickness pushed aside by a rush of activity.

passage:
Supervisor's note, design internship, end of week three
Ayesha, who moved from Lucknow for this internship, has been late twice this week. On Monday she explained she'd spent the weekend flat-hunting because the paying guest place had no water in the mornings. On Wednesday she lost an hour at the bank trying to open an account; they wanted a local address proof she doesn't have yet. She told Kamal at lunch, loudly, that the biryani here "isn't biryani," that people here speak too fast, and that in Lucknow an auto driver would never cheat you. Kamal laughed, but she wasn't joking. Her work is still good, but she sighs at small things, a jammed printer, a wrong cable.
What I did next: I gave her Friday afternoon off to sort the bank, wrote a letter confirming her internship address, and told her that the first month in a new city wears most people down.

qa.q: Why did the bank refuse to open Ayesha's account on Wednesday?
qa.a: They wanted a local address proof she doesn't have yet.

qa.q: How is Ayesha feeling after three weeks in the new city?
qa.a: Ayesha feels worn down and irritable, frustrated by flat-hunting and paperwork, and keeps comparing everything unfavourably with Lucknow.

qa.q: What turning point did the supervisor offer, and why does it help?
qa.a: The supervisor removed practical blocks by giving time off and an address letter, and normalised the tough first month, which eases the pile-up of small irritations.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel when Ayesha complains about the biryani?
qa.a: Kamal may feel a little stung on behalf of the city but also sympathetic, sensing that she is tired rather than truly angry at Kamal.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new city worn down by flat, food, language and paperwork, with small irritations piling up and constant comparison with home.

passage: The power went out across the hostel in Pune at nine, the week of Durga Puja, and Bidisha lay on her bed in the dark with her phone at eleven percent. Back in Kolkata, her family would be at the pandal right now, her Thakuma in her white-and-red saree, her cousins arguing over rolls. Here, nobody had even heard of the sweet she had searched three markets for. Her classmates were friendly, but no one knew that she hated coriander or that she sang when she was nervous. She felt like a guest in her own life. She tried to call home, but the network dropped twice. She started crying quietly, then harder. Her roommate Shalini sat up in the dark. "Homesick?" Bidisha nodded, then realised Shalini couldn't see. "Yes." "Me too, last year. It passes. It doesn't mean you shouldn't have come."

qa.q: What was Bidisha's phone battery at when the power went out?
qa.a: Her phone was at eleven percent.

qa.q: What is Bidisha feeling as she lies in the dark?
qa.a: Bidisha feels homesick and sad, missing her family at the pandal and feeling like an outsider where no one knows her.

qa.q: What could help Bidisha after this night?
qa.a: Talking more with Shalini, planning a proper call home, and finding a small local puja gathering could help her feel less alone without deciding the move was wrong.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel hearing Bidisha cry?
qa.a: Shalini probably feels sympathetic, remembering that same homesickness from last year, and wants Bidisha to know the feeling passes.

grounding: Shows a young adult weeks after a move missing family, food and being known, crying at night, and hearing that this does not mean the move was wrong.

passage: I'm Hrithik. In my first term at college in Bengaluru, I called home one Sunday and couldn't hide how flat I sounded. Papa heard it straight away. "You're tired, beta?" I said I was fine. Later, Ma told me he'd sat on the balcony for an hour after that call, not saying much. I didn't know parents missed you like that. After that, Papa called every Sunday at eight. He never said "come home" or "we're so lonely without you." He asked what I ate, whether my roommate Deepak still snored, how the chemistry lab went. Sometimes he'd send a photo of the neighbour's cat on our wall. I knew he was worried; he just didn't make it my job to fix. Looking back, those calls were like a rope I could hold. I stayed, I settled, and I still knew exactly where home was.

qa.q: At what time did Papa call every Sunday?
qa.a: Papa called every Sunday at eight.

qa.q: What does Papa sitting on the balcony for an hour suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Papa felt worried and sad, missing his child and anxious after hearing Hrithik sound low.

qa.q: What made Papa's calls helpful rather than heavy?
qa.a: They were regular and warm, asked about daily things, and carried no guilt-tripping or demands to return, so Hrithik could settle while keeping a base.

qa.q: How might the calls have been different if Papa had said we're so lonely without you?
qa.a: Hrithik might have felt guilty and torn about staying, making it harder to settle in Bengaluru.

grounding: Shows parents feeling a child's absence and worrying when the young person sounds low, and a parent's regular, warm calls without guilt or pressure giving the young person a base.

subtype: Stage 4: Loneliness and testing the new place [Actor]
passage: Wei had been in Madrid for four months, working at an engineering firm near the river. His colleagues were friendly: Rosa always said "¡Buenos días!" and asked about his weekend. But after work everyone went home to families or old friends, and Wei's weekends stretched out empty and grey. He tried the neighbourhood running club; the runners were kind but fast, and chatted in quick Spanish he couldn't follow. He went to a Chinese community association's dumpling evening, and found he had more in common with the grandmothers than with anyone his age. Last Saturday he ate paella alone and watched couples on the terraces. On Monday Rosa mentioned a Thursday board-game night at a bar. Wei almost said no. Then he thought about the months ahead and said he'd come. It would take time, he knew now. Not weeks. Months.

qa.q: What did Wei eat alone last Saturday?
qa.a: He ate paella alone and watched couples on the terraces.

qa.q: How does Wei feel about his weekends in Madrid?
qa.a: Wei feels lonely and a little discouraged, with weekends stretching empty while everyone else goes home to families or old friends.

qa.q: What is Wei learning about making friends in a new place, and what could he keep doing?
qa.a: He is learning that friendships take months, so he could keep saying yes to regular things like the Thursday board-game night and the running club.

qa.q: How might Rosa see Wei when she mentions the board-game night?
qa.a: Rosa probably sees a friendly but lonely colleague and wants to include him, perhaps unsure whether he'll come.

grounding: Shows a newcomer finding colleagues friendly but distant and weekends empty, trying clubs and community groups, and learning that friendships take months.

passage: In the second month of her job in Hyderabad, Trisha caught a fever the same week her first big presentation was torn apart by the client. She lay in her rented flat in Madhapur, sweating under two blankets, too weak to cook. There was no one to bring her rasam. Her phone showed messages from the office group about the presentation's "learnings." She thought, maybe I should just go back to Nagpur. Maybe this whole move was a mistake. At midnight, she scrolled to Maria, a colleague who had once shared lunch with her. She typed, "Sorry to bother, I'm unwell. Do you know a clinic nearby?" and almost deleted it. She sent it. Maria replied in five minutes: "Not a bother! There's one on my street. I'll take you tomorrow morning, and I'm bringing soup." Trisha put the phone on her chest and cried with relief.

qa.q: How quickly did Maria reply?
qa.a: Maria replied in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling before she sent the message to Maria?
qa.a: Trisha felt low and doubtful, sick and alone, wondering whether the whole move to Hyderabad had been a mistake.

qa.q: Why did the midnight message matter so much?
qa.a: Reaching out, even hesitantly, connected Trisha to someone who could help, which turned a very low week and gave her some support in the new city.

qa.q: How might Maria feel getting Trisha's message at midnight?
qa.a: Maria may feel concerned but glad to be asked, seeing it as a chance to help a new colleague who has no one nearby.

grounding: Shows a bad week of illness and a work setback in an unfamiliar city, doubt about the move peaking, and reaching out to someone turning the stretch.

passage:
Note by Siddharth, team lead, three months after Anirban joined our Chennai office
When Anirban arrived from Kolkata in March, he ate at his desk and left at six sharp. I've noticed a real change since. He now goes to the same small café on Kutchery Road every morning; the owner starts his filter coffee when he walks in. He joined the office badminton group on Tuesdays and Fridays. He's learning Tamil phrases from our receptionist and practises them on the auto drivers, who seem to enjoy correcting him. On Sundays, he told me, he still makes luchi and aloo dum the way his mother does, and video-calls home while he eats. He seems steadier at work too, speaking up more in reviews.
What I did next: I asked him to show the two new joiners from Delhi around next week, since he knows now what the first month feels like.

qa.q: On which days does Anirban play badminton?
qa.a: He plays with the office badminton group on Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: How does Anirban seem to feel now compared with March?
qa.a: Anirban seems steadier and more settled, relaxed enough to speak up more at work and enjoy practising Tamil.

qa.q: Which routines have helped Anirban, and why?
qa.a: A regular café, badminton twice a week, learning local phrases and keeping his Sunday luchi ritual from home give steady rhythms while new ties grow.

qa.q: How might the two new joiners from Delhi experience Anirban's help?
qa.a: They may feel welcomed and reassured, having someone who remembers how the first month feels to guide them around.

grounding: Shows a newcomer finding a regular café and sports group, learning local ways and keeping home rituals, building steadiness while new ties form.

passage: I'm Alka. Fourteen months ago I got off the train in Guwahati with two suitcases and no idea how to say thank you in Assamese. Now the vegetable seller keeps the best lemons for me, I have a Saturday walking group by the Brahmaputra, and I dream in a mix of languages. When I go home to Jaipur, I miss the rain here, and when I'm here, I miss Maa's dal baati. I used to think that meant I didn't belong anywhere. Now I think it means I belong in two places. Last month a new engineer, Darshan, joined our office from Pune, looking exactly how I must have looked: lost, polite, eating lunch alone. I took Darshan to the lemon seller, and to the walking group. It felt like paying back something both cities had given me.

qa.q: How long ago did Alka arrive in Guwahati?
qa.a: Alka arrived fourteen months ago.

qa.q: How does Alka feel about having two places to miss?
qa.a: Alka feels grateful and at peace, seeing it as belonging in two places rather than nowhere.

qa.q: How is Alka helping Darshan, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Alka introduces Darshan to the lemon seller and the walking group, passing on the small routines and ties that helped Alka settle.

qa.q: What might Darshan be experiencing in these first weeks?
qa.a: Darshan is probably feeling lost and lonely, eating lunch alone, and relieved to have someone show the way.

grounding: Shows a person who, after about a year, feels at home in two places, keeps ties to both with gratitude and helps a newcomer through the same path.
